issues.legal_issue: A partner’s interest in partnership assets that include immovable property is a movable interest in the partnership as a whole, not an interest in any specific asset.
material_facts: Two families carried on a joint business as partners, each holding a half share.
The partnership assets included land brought into the business and land acquired during the business.
The dispute concerned how a partner’s interest in those assets should be characterized for registration purposes.
issues.conclusion: A partner’s interest in partnership assets, including immovable property, is to be treated as movable property; during the partnership the partner has no right to any specific item, and on dissolution or retirement the partner is entitled to the money value of the share in the net assets after liabilities and prior charges.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 14 and 15 of the Partnership Act, property brought into or acquired for the firm’s business is partnership property and is held and used for that business. Sections 29, 30, 37 and 48 show that a partner’s rights concern profits during the partnership and, on dissolution or retirement, the value of the share after the firm’s liabilities and prior charges are addressed, rather than ownership of a specific asset. The Court relied on Lindley on Partnership and authorities including Rodriguez v. Speyer Bros. and Darby v. Darby, and approved the view that partnership assets must be realized and applied in settling the partners’ accounts.

predicates.registration_issue_in_partnership_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in which the registration treatment of a partner’s interest in partnership assets is disputed.
predicates.partnership_assets_used_for_joint_busine: The partners brought property into or acquired property for use in their joint business.
predicates.partnership_assets_include_immovable_pro: The assets of the partnership included immovable property.

issues.definition: When an appeal disputes registration treatment of a partner’s interest in joint-business assets that include immovable property, the partner’s interest is treated as movable property.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered deed recording the end of a partnership and a partner’s relinquishment of a general share in the business does not require registration merely because the partnership owned immovable property, where it does not convey any specific immovable property.
material_facts: The defendants relied on an unregistered deed to show that the partnership had ended and its accounts had been settled.
The deed recorded that one family had given up its share in the machinery and business to the other family.
The deed did not expressly refer to or convey any specific immovable property; its reference to property concerned property already delivered earlier.
The partnership had owned immovable property.
issues.conclusion: The deed was admissible in evidence to prove the dissolution and settlement, notwithstanding that the partnership owned immovable property, because it did not convey immovable property expressly or by necessary implication.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(1)(c) of the Registration Act, 1908 requires registration of an instrument that creates, declares, assigns, limits or extinguishes an interest in immovable property. A partner’s share is an interest in the partnership’s net assets, not an interest in a specific partnership asset. The Court relied on the reasoning in Chitturi Venkataratnam v. Siram Subba Rao and distinguished agreements that expressly or by necessary implication require a party to convey an interest in land, as discussed in Gray v. Smith.

issues.definition: If an appeal disputes an unregistered deed concerning a partnership with immovable assets, the deed records termination and a general release, does not convey specific immovable property, and mentions only an earlier property delivery, it is admissible to prove dissolution and settlement.
